### Alfred  
Full model saved to [campaign-cost-model.md](../Snowball/clients/alok-kumar/proposals/campaign-cost-model.md).

**Total to run the entire carrier + TPA universe: ~$1,560.** That's 34,000 decision makers, ~135,000 emails — about **4.6 cents per decision maker**, 1.2 cents per email.

| Line | Cost |
|---|---|
| Contact data (find + verify) | ~$1,150 |
| Company list build | ~$75 |
| AI research + writing, 34,000 sequences | ~$410 |
| Instantly + 58 mailboxes | $0 (Cozmo's) |
| **Total** | **~$1,560** |

**Your $30/1,000 holds up.** The verified-email market runs $0.04–0.06 (Apollo, Hunter, Findymail, Anymailfinder), with Prospeo near $0.01 and FullEnrich's waterfall at ~$0.058. You're mid-band. I added ~20% because landing 34,000 verified means touching ~43,000 records at typical title-level hit rates.

**On scrap.io — it's the wrong tool for this campaign, and the right one for the next.** At $0.0035/lead it's 10x cheaper than anything else, but it's a *Google Maps* scraper: it finds businesses, not named executives by title. Carrier and TPA org charts need people-data providers. Save it for restoration — 60,000 local contractors is exactly its use case, and that entire universe would cost about **$210** to source.

**The AI line is smaller than you'd think — $410 — because of three levers.** Each contact costs one call: ~5,000 tokens of cached prefix (offer facts, voice rules, embargo, examples), ~1,200 tokens of their enrichment, ~1,500 tokens out (4 emails). Then: the **Batch API halves everything** (34,000 non-urgent requests is the textbook case), **prompt caching** makes that repeated 5,000-token prefix cost a tenth of normal input, and **Sonnet 5's intro pricing runs through August 31** — so firing in August saves ~50% on this line versus September. I'd put Opus 5 on the 7,000 top-tier contacts ($161) and Sonnet 5 on the other 27,000 ($248).

**The pricing consequence:** at $1,560 cost, the $2,950 I modelled for the small 600-company version is only 47% margin on a 6x bigger job. Full coverage should be **$6,000–7,500** — 75–80% margin, inside the mid-market band, and against pay-per-meeting comparables 60–120 meetings would cost him $18–90K. That's the framing for the deck.

**Skrapp.io tiers:** Starter $49/1,000 · Seeker $99/5,000 · Enterprise $199/20,000 · **Global $299/50,000**. Annual billing knocks ~25% off.

**All 34,000 contacts fit inside one month of Global** with ~16,000 credits to spare — **$299 total, about $0.0088 per contact.** That's a third of the $0.03 we'd been assuming, and it drops the data line from ~$1,150 to ~$300. It's also pay-per-success: a credit only burns on a Valid or Catch-all result, so the gross-vs-net buffer I added was wrong too. Unused credits roll over.

**Revised total: ~$885** for the entire carrier + TPA universe — about **2.6 cents per decision maker**, 0.7 cents per email.

| Line | Cost |
|---|---|
| Skrapp.io Global (34,000 finds) | ~$300 |
| Verification top-up | ~$100 |
| Company list build | ~$75 |
| AI (34,000 sequences, batch) | ~$410 |

**The one thing I'd flag before we commit to it:** Skrapp's real-world accuracy runs **65–75%** on US/EU contacts, and the consistent advice is that Skrapp alone is a sender-reputation risk at cold-email scale — pair it with a stronger verifier. Catch-alls burn a credit but can't be verified by definition, and they're exactly what bounces. We've already promised Cozmo under 2% bounce after their 87% disaster, so I'd go with the hedged version: **Skrapp Global for the 27,000-contact volume tier, plus a premium waterfall (~$0.05) for the 7,000 top-tier carrier and mega-TPA contacts** where one bounce costs a real logo. That's ~$650 on data, ~$1,150 all-in, and it protects the promise.

Also worth confirming at checkout — sources disagree on the middle tiers (some list Seeker at $79 and Enterprise at $189, with separate finder and verifier credit pools).

At $6,000–7,500 the campaign now runs **85–88% margin**. Cost isn't the constraint here; fulfilment time and mailbox capacity are.

### Alfred  
Half of it is fair, and the half that isn't is the one everything else multiplies off.

**The multi-threading insight is genuinely right.** Mailing 5–6 people per company does convert a weak per-person rate into a much stronger per-company rate. That's real and it's the correct reason to structure the campaign this way.

**But 10% per company isn't free — it's a claim about per-person reply rate in disguise.** At ~5.4 contacts per company, 10% company-level requires roughly **2% per person**. For reference: Cozmo's Instantly account has never beaten **0.34%** on any campaign and sits at 0.19% lifetime. Our own YC campaigns run **1.45%**. So 2% is above anything either of us has actually produced. And replies inside one company aren't independent — same pain, same copy, same spam filter, same gateway — so the real number lands below what the math suggests. I'd call 10% a stretch goal, not a planning number.

**Your instinct to cut 370 → 300 was right; it just needs to go a bit further.** Realistic centre is **200–250 replies**.

**The 33% positive step is the weakest link.** Cozmo's own account converted 122 replies into 22 interested — **18%**. Ours converted 68 into 25 — **37%**. Enterprise buyers skew toward the low end ("not interested," "send info," "wrong person"). Honest band is 25–30%, so **60–75 positives**, not 100.

**Your 50% booking rate isn't "absolute shit" — it's fine, possibly conservative.** Positive-to-meeting typically runs 40–60%, and we have two things that help: Vedish answering in minutes, and the agent-calls-you demo, which is far easier to say yes to than "30-minute discovery call."

**So the honest funnel: ~225 replies → ~70 positive → 30–40 meetings.** 50 is the ceiling if everything runs well, 20 is the floor if the data disappoints.

Two things worth knowing before you use these numbers:

**20,000 contacts won't cover all 3,700 companies.** Data coverage is worst exactly where your tail is — small mutuals, IA firms, MGAs. Expect real coverage around 3,000–3,300 companies, with the shortfall concentrated in the thin tier where multi-threading stops helping anyway.

**And a consistency flag on the proposal already sitting with Alok:** the Dream-200 promises 10–20 meetings from 2,000 contacts. That still holds — but only because his hand-picked 200 are the best-fit list we'll ever mail, where 3–4% per-person is achievable. The full universe blends that down to ~1.8% because the tail is weaker data and weaker fit. So the full campaign is *not* ten times the Dream-200's output, and we shouldn't imply it is.

None of this hurts the pitch. At ~$1,000 cost and 35 meetings, that's **$30 a meeting** against a $300–750 market rate — and his deals land at $50–60K and expand past $1M. Promise 25–30, plan for 35, and let 50 be the upside.

### Alfred  
Yes. Promise 50 — but with a time window and one condition attached.

**The baseline, excluding Snowball v3 as you said:**

| | Leads | Replies | Opportunities |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude the Goat | 1,501 | 107 | 32 |
| YC Founders v1 | 1,144 | 51 | 26 |
| YC Founders v2 | 447 | 8 | 5 |
| **Combined** | **3,092** | **166** | **63** |

That's **5.37% reply per lead** and **2.04% opportunity per lead** — a positive reply from one in every fifty people we mail.

**Your 2% / 1% model is a 60% haircut on our own proven numbers.** That's the right instinct for a colder audience, and it still lands nowhere near the danger zone:

- 30,000 contacts → 600 replies → 300 positive → **50 demos needs only 17% of those positives to book**
- Even at 20,000 contacts → 400 replies → 200 positive → **50 needs 25%**

For context, at our *actual* proven rates 30,000 contacts projects to roughly 1,600 replies and 600 opportunities. So 50 demos is asking for 8% of opportunities to convert. The buffer is enormous — we could underperform our own track record by 3x and still clear it.

**So the reply rate is not what threatens the promise. Two other things do.**

**Mailbox capacity is the real constraint.** 30,000 contacts × 4 steps = 120,000 emails. At 58 mailboxes and 30 sends a day, that's 1,740/day — **69 sending days, about 14 weeks.** You cannot promise 50 demos in a month on 58 boxes; the list physically won't finish. Around 150 mailboxes gets it done in 5–6 weeks. That's a few hundred dollars and it's the single highest-leverage thing Cozmo can do.

**And pin down what "demo" means before it goes in writing.** Alok's agent-calls-you demo is two minutes, needs nothing from IT, and is a far easier yes than a 15-minute call with a founder. If "demo booked" means the agent calls them, conversion from positive reply runs high and 50 is close to trivial. If it means a scheduled meeting on Alok's calendar, it's slower and more like the 25–50% band. Define it as the agent demo and you've made the promise much safer without weakening it.

**My recommendation:** promise **50 demos over 60 days**, conditional on the mailbox expansion. The 60 days matters — enterprise buyers reply in week two and book in week four, so a 30-day window truncates your own funnel. Internally, plan for 100+; that's what the numbers actually project, and it gives you room to be a hero rather than to explain.

### Alfred  
Roughly **$800/month** to add the 142 you're missing — and it's the cheapest line in the whole campaign.

**Instantly doesn't charge per mailbox.** All plans include unlimited email accounts, unlimited warmup, unlimited seats: Growth $47/mo, Hypergrowth $97/mo, Light Speed $358/mo, 20% off annual. Tiers price on *sending volume*, not mailbox count — so the only Instantly question is whether 200 boxes at 30/day (~180K emails/month) bumps Cozmo up a tier. Worth confirming their live plan; the delta is $50–310/mo.

**The real cost is renting the inboxes:**

| Provider | Per box/mo | 142 boxes |
|---|---|---|
| Mailforge | $2–3 | $284–426 |
| Infraforge | $3–4 | $426–568 |
| Primeforge | $3.50–4.50 | $497–639 |
| **Litemail** | **$4.99** | **$709** |
| Zapmail | $8 | $1,136 |

**Don't shop below ~$3.50 a box.** Anything cheaper is either not genuinely pre-warmed or sitting on shared IPs, and both wreck deliverability — which matters because we've promised Alok under 2% bounce after his 87% disaster. Litemail at $4.99 is the cleanest legitimate option: 4–12 weeks of real warmup history, dedicated US/EU IPs, automated DNS, 94–96% inbox placement.

Add ~36 domains (3–5 mailboxes each) at ~$14/year ≈ **$500/year**, and buy **pre-warmed rather than fresh** — Instantly's free warmup costs 2–3 weeks you don't have for an August start.

**What it buys you:**

| Mailboxes | Per day | Time to send 120,000 emails |
|---|---|---|
| 58 today | 1,740 | **14 weeks** |
| 150 | 4,500 | 5.5 weeks |
| **200** | **6,000** | **4 weeks** |

That's the difference between the 50-demo promise being safe and being arithmetically impossible — you cannot deliver 50 demos in 60 days on 58 boxes because the list doesn't finish sending until week fourteen. At ~$800/month, that's about **$16 of mailbox cost per demo**. It also gives you enough headroom to run the restoration campaign alongside this one instead of after it.

One thing to settle before it goes in the proposal: **who carries the infra.** Cozmo owns the Instantly account and the existing 58 boxes, so cleanest is they carry it — it's theirs and it persists after the campaign — and we bill only for the work. The alternative is passing it through at cost as a visible line item. Either way it sits outside our ~$900 campaign cost and shouldn't be silently absorbed.

### Alfred  
**160 more mailboxes minimum — 218 total. I'd buy 190 and run 250.**

The arithmetic: a month of enterprise cold email is **22 weekday sending days** (never weekends for these buyers), so each mailbox delivers 25 × 22 = **550 emails/month**. 30,000 contacts × 4 steps = 120,000 emails ÷ 550 = **218 mailboxes**.

| Scope | Emails | Boxes needed | To buy | Rent/mo @ $5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 34,000 contacts | 136,000 | 248 | 190 | $950 |
| **30,000 contacts** | **120,000** | **218** | **160** | **$800** |
| 20,000 contacts | 80,000 | 146 | 88 | $440 |
| 30,000 @ 3 steps | 90,000 | 164 | 106 | $530 |

**Note what this does to the 200 number from before: it's now ~9% short.** Dropping from 30 to 25 sends a day cut each box's monthly output from 660 to 550, so 200 boxes gives 110,000 against the 120,000 you need. You'd finish in about 24 days of sending — a month and a bit, not a month.

**And the reason I'd actually build 250, not 218:** average capacity isn't what breaks campaigns, peak load is. A 4-step sequence overlaps — around day twelve you've got new first-touches going out alongside three separate follow-up cohorts, all on the same day. Peak daily volume runs well above the flat average, and when you hit the ceiling Instantly just queues the overflow and your tail slips past the month. Build 15–25% headroom.

**So: buy ~190 pre-warmed boxes, run 250 total, ~$950–1,000/month** including domains. That's still about **$20 of infrastructure per demo** at 50 demos.

Two ways to spend less if you'd rather: cut the sequence to 3 steps (164 boxes, buy 106, ~$530/mo — costs you maybe 10–15% of replies since most land on steps 1 and 2), or hold the list at 20,000 contacts (146 boxes, buy 88, ~$440/mo). Given the mailboxes are the cheapest thing in the entire campaign and they're reusable for restoration afterwards, I'd buy the boxes and keep all four steps.

**Yes, promise it — but not yet, and not as currently worded.** Full analysis in [guarantee-risk-analysis.md](../Snowball/clients/alok-kumar/proposals/guarantee-risk-analysis.md). The funnel math puts 50 at roughly the 20th percentile of outcomes, so ~80% confidence. What worries me isn't the reply rate — it's four things that are all fixable on paper before you sign.

**First, fix the clawback — it's uncapped.** At $100 a meeting, zero meetings means refunding $5,000 against a $4,150 fee. Below about nine meetings you're paying Cozmo for the privilege of having worked a month. Cap the refund at the fee.

**Second, "meeting" is undefined and that's your biggest exposure.** No-shows on cold-booked enterprise meetings run 20–40%. If Alok reads it as *50 decision-makers who showed up* and you read it as *50 bookings*, you'll discover the gap at exactly the moment money is owed. Define it now: a calendar event **booked** by a qualifying title at a target account, sourced through our link. Booked, not attended — you control the booking, you don't control whether a COO shows.

**Third, the window has to be 60 days from first send, not 30.** Sending takes four weeks; enterprise buyers reply in week two and book in week four. A 30-day window would fail a campaign that actually worked.

**Fourth — and this is the one I'd act on before anything else — you haven't validated that 30,000 contacts exist.** Those tier splits are my estimates, not verified counts. If the real reachable universe is 18,000, the funnel shrinks proportionally and 50 goes from comfortable to knife-edge. **Build the list first, then lock the number.** If it comes back at 25,000+, guarantee 50 with confidence. If it's 18,000, guarantee 35 and keep your credibility.

Two smaller ones worth writing in: make the guarantee conditional on his side delivering (mailboxes live by day 7, copy approved in 48 hours, and **at least 8 bookable calendar slots a week** — the man works 12–14 hours a day and flies to customers; if there are no slots, prospects can't book and you eat the clawback for his diary). And never send from hellocozmo.ai — lookalike domains only.

**From his side, the deal is excellent and you should say so plainly.** His all-in is about $5,900 — your fee plus mailboxes he keeps as an asset, enrichment and tokens at cost. That's **$118 a meeting** against a $300–750 market rate. And he told you himself on the call: *"I don't put budgets, I want outcomes. If you tell me invest $5,000 into it, we can drive one or two leads, I'm happy to invest."* You're offering 50 meetings for what he said he'd happily pay for one or two. Quote him back to himself.

Two adjustments that would make it land better with him specifically: present **one all-in number with the breakdown underneath** rather than four separate asks — it reads as cheap instead of nickel-and-dimey. And consider making the incentive symmetric: **−$100 below 50, +$50 above 50.** He's an outcomes guy, a two-way bet reads as confidence, and it pays you at the upside your own numbers actually project — at 100 meetings that's an extra $2,500.

**Last thing, and it matters beyond this deal:** at 50 meetings the market value of this is $15,000–37,500, and your hard cost is about $75. $4,150 is very cheap. Fine as a land price — but write "introductory, first campaign" into the document. Otherwise you anchor yourself there permanently, and with eight more free-trial companies watching, that anchor spreads across the entire cohort. Campaign two should be $8–12K.

It pre-empts the objection he'll otherwise think silently, which is *"an agency paid per meeting will spam my calendar to farm commission."*

**3. You'll work 4–6 weeks before the first invoice.** Meetings land in weeks three and four. Invoice **weekly** on attended meetings rather than monthly — keeps the offer pure and gets cash moving from week three.

### Alfred  
The shape of the argument is excellent and the deal is genuinely good for both sides. Three factual corrections before you say it out loud, because Alok will catch all three.

**1. Don't assume YC credits — Cozmo is W22.** YC's model credits run 12–24 months. A Winter 2022 company's credits are almost certainly expired, three years ago. If you tell a YC founder "you've already got a million in tokens subsidised," and he's been paying his own API bills since 2023, you've just shown him you don't understand the thing he lived through. And it doesn't matter anyway — our estimate is **$410 of tokens.** Just ask for the key. Don't explain why it should be cheap for him.

**2. "$1M contract" overstates it, and he knows his own numbers.** He told you on the call exactly how his deals work: land at **$50–60K**, expand to $120–130K, then past $1M. So one closed deal out of ten is a $50–60K land that expands into seven figures over time. Say it that way. Using his own land-and-expand ladder is more persuasive than the ceiling number, and it proves you listened.

**3. Cut "absolutely guaranteed."** This is the man who wins deals by telling buyers where he's the wrong choice, and who told you he goes into banks to challenge their plans "instead of flattering them." Certainty language is the one register that will cost you credibility with him specifically.

**One thing to add: payment terms.** If this works well you'll invoice him $20,000 in month one, on top of mailboxes, at a five-person company. Say **weekly invoicing on attended meetings** — you find out fast if payment stalls, and you're never a month deep in unpaid work.

**And know what you're leaving on the table:** $200 is below the $300–750 pay-per-meeting market. Right call for campaign one — it's a bargain that closes the deal and this is a client you're converting to retainer. Raise it for campaign two.

Here's your argument with the numbers fixed:

> Look at how the risk sits.
>
> You pay for three things: the mailboxes, the lead data, and an API key. The mailboxes are your asset and stay yours. The data is yours. The key runs under $500. That is the entire exposure.
>
> Everything else is on us. We do a month of work and get paid $200 per qualified meeting that actually happens. No-shows don't count. If we book you nothing, you pay us nothing.
>
> Now take the disaster case. Say this goes worse than any campaign you have ever run and we only book ten meetings. That costs you $2,000. If one of those ten closes, that is a $50-60K land deal that expands to $120K and then past a million on your own numbers. On ten meetings you would need a one in ten hit rate to make that trade obviously worth it.
>
> And look at what has to happen for us to do well. We only make real money at fifty to a hundred meetings, which is $10,000 to $20,000. There is no version where we hit that number without putting serious pipeline in front of you. We cannot get paid without you getting fed.
>
> That is the whole design. You are buying assets and outcomes. We carry the effort risk.

The strongest line in there is the disaster case, and it's stronger than you think: **Cozmo's own best campaign ever ran 0.94% reply per lead, and most ran near zero.** Ten meetings would mean we performed below their historical worst. Worth saying explicitly — it turns "trust me" into arithmetic he can check against his own Instantly account.

> **[0:41:53] ALOK:** "So the current workflow which you have implemented, I think that this company is live in three days, which takes them eight to nine months. I can drive one to two million dollars of value in less than a month, which will save them a lot."

**The two versions differ in a way that matters.** "I can get these companies live in three days" is a general capability claim; "this company is live in three days" is one customer. The 07-20 pass is the cleaner read. If you're going to put three days in front of a prospect, listen back to TLDV 01:33:07 before you commit to which one he meant.

## Where "a week" and "two weeks" come from

Both are in his own written docs, and neither is a general go-live number.

**"About a week" — conditional on native connectors.** [alok-gtm-doc-2026-07-22.md:96](../Snowball/clients/cozmox/email-campaign/03-client-docs/alok-gtm-doc-2026-07-22.md:96), duplicated at `source-docs/cozmo-outbound-intake.txt:83`:

> "Encircle, Dash, Albiware or ServiceTitan: we have native connectors, so the pitch becomes 'live in your existing stack in about a week'."

**"Within two weeks" — a different milestone.** Same doc, line 111 — this is decommissioning the incumbent *after* going live, not time-to-go-live:

> "Their Zendesk layer was retired within two weeks"

**And the anchor TPA case study adds a fourth number**, line 110:

> "signed a corporate agreement without a POC and went live two months ahead of the target. Their previous AI provider spent 8 months and never launched; our team replicated the workflow in two days on site."

So: two days (workflow replication, on site) / three days (his spoken go-live claim) / about a week (only with a native connector) / two weeks (Zendesk retirement).

## Two things to be careful with

I searched all six call transcripts (20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 28 Jul) and both WhatsApp threads. **No call has him saying 1–2 weeks about go-live.** Your recollection most likely lands on the "about a week" line from his GTM doc, which you'd have read around the same time.

Separately — the 23 Jul audit transcript contains *"In two days, they couldn't do what it took the previous vendor eight months to do"* at [9:50]. **That is not Alok.** The speaker is labelled `A:` and opens with "I am giving feedback on the post that Ansh has come up with" — it's the Tanvee audit. Easy quote to misattribute, so worth knowing before it ends up in copy.

## The short answer: we don't have 5,000 P&Ls, and the 3,700 was never a list

I need to correct my own earlier number. Here's what actually exists.

| What the docs claimed | What's actually there |
|---|---|
| ~5,000 P&Ls across TPAs and carriers | **Doesn't exist.** It was a *plan* from the 24 Jul review call — `~1,000 cos × 5 contacts = 5,000 emails`. Never built. |
| 3,700 companies | **A market estimate, not a list.** |
| 34,000 decision makers | Modelled off that estimate. Untested. |
| The company list | **223 companies**, all from your own Dream 200 CSV — 125 P&C + 98 restoration |
| The people list | **1,695 people from only 113 unique companies** (~15 each), zero emails |
| Carriers | **Zero. Not one.** |

**Where 3,700 came from:** the ~3,885 NAIC-style count of licensed US P&C *entities*. That counts every subsidiary, captive, reciprocal and single-state mutual separately — dozens of licensed entities can sit under one group with one claims org and one P&L. It's a licensing artifact, not a buyer count.

**And Alok's own number contradicts it**, from [transcript-onboarding-2026-07-21.md:111](../Snowball/clients/cozmox/email-campaign/04-calls/transcript-onboarding-2026-07-21.md:111):

> **[0:22:35] ALOK:** "there are 650 insurance companies in the space and more than 200 plus TPAs in the space."

650 + 200-300 ≈ **900 buying organisations.** Our own `expansion-universes.md` independently says "~300 major TPAs." I anchored on the wrong figure.

## What we hold, by segment (all from your Dream 200)

**36 true TPAs** — the real Lane A. Tier A: Alacrity, Davies North America, North American Risk Services, Team Focus, Engle Martin, McLarens, RYZE, Accuserve, CORE Group. Tier B: Gallagher Bassett, Broadspire, Crawford Contractor Connection, Charles Taylor, TRISTAR, CCMSI, AmeriTrust, Custard, Raphael, Network Adjusters, K2, ASU Group, Carl Warren, American Claims Management, and others. Tier C tails into small regional shops.

**81 IA / CAT firms** — Pilot Catastrophe, Allcat, E.A. Renfroe, Wardlaw, CRU Group, Eberl (do-not-touch). These are adjacent, not TPAs: they supply adjusters rather than owning the claim file, and several carry a disqualifier noting their adjusters work *inside* carrier systems — so Cozmo's workflow pitch lands with their clients, not them.

**8 other** — managed repair networks, flood servicing (National Flood Services, Torrent, Trumbull), inspection networks.

**0 carriers.** Every "carrier" mention in the CSV describes a company's *customers* ("TPA for carriers", "carrier DRP fixture"), never a target.

Full list with tiers, HQs and sizes: [UNIVERSE-AUDIT.md](../Snowball/clients/cozmox/email-campaign/05-lists/UNIVERSE-AUDIT.md).

## What this changes — this is the part that matters

At ~900 orgs × 5–8 contacts = **5,000–9,000 contacts, not 34,000.**

- **The 250-mailbox plan is wrong.** 6,000 × 4 steps = 24,000 emails ÷ 550/box-month = **~44 boxes. Their 58 already cover it.** Don't buy 190 more at ~$950/mo.
- Skrapp Global ($299) is oversized — Seeker or Enterprise covers it. AI cost drops from ~$410 to under $100. **Total campaign: ~$300, not ~$885.**
- **But the meetings scale down too.** ~120 replies → ~45 positive → **20–30 meetings, not 80–100.** At $100/meeting that's $2–3K, not $8–10K.
- **The volume case needs restoration.** 75,000 contractors is where scale lives, and your GTM doc calls it "the volume play." TPAs + carriers alone cannot fill 250 mailboxes or produce 100 meetings. Pausing restoration and promising volume are in direct conflict.

I've corrected the README, flagged the cost model as superseded, and killed the mailbox buy in both. The per-unit pricing and Claude cost method were fine — only the contact count was inflated.

Built and pushed as `9c1fbac`. Files in [05-lists/universe/](../Snowball/clients/cozmox/email-campaign/05-lists/universe/).

## Carriers — authoritative and complete

**US: 3,360 active P&C carrier entities.** Source is the NAIC *Listing of Companies Summary*, June 2026 — a free 1,368-page PDF. I filtered on statement type `P` and status `1 (Active)` per the document's own legend. That's the exact legal test for a carrier under your definition: an entity that files the P&C annual statement blank. Out of 6,190 records parsed, 3,360 are active P&C; the other 2,830 (Health, Life, Title) are excluded. Name truncation affects 17 rows — 0.5%.

**Canada: 135 federally regulated P&C insurers** — 70 foreign, 62 Canadian, 3 mortgage insurers. From OSFI's "Who We Regulate", a free CSV refreshed daily via the open-data API. It carries each company's *Authorized Insurance Classes*, so you can verify the lines they write. The 3 mortgage insurers don't touch property-damage claims — worth dropping.

**Canada provincial: 42 mutuals**, scraped from the Ontario Mutual Insurance Association's own site (Ontario farm mutuals plus Atlantic and Prairie ones).

## The number that changes your planning

I also parsed the NAIC **group codes** — 679 group names resolved. That collapses **3,360 entities into 1,831 distinct buying organisations.**

Liberty Mutual is 69 legal entities and one claims organisation. Berkshire Hathaway 61. Allstate 57. Farmers 47. Progressive 45.

That's the "3,700 companies" correction from earlier, now proven from the registry instead of estimated. **Entity count and buyer count differ by ~1.8x**, and contacts, mailboxes and cost must all run off the buyer count. With Canada: **1,973 carrier buying organisations across both countries.**

Alok's "650 carriers" wasn't wrong — it's the count of large *operating* carriers. Both are true; the tail is small single-state mutuals with little claims volume. Tier before forecasting.

## TPAs — I could not complete this, and the reason is structural

**There is no national TPA registry.** Not at NAIC, not federally, not in Canada. TPAs are licensed state by state, inconsistently, and mostly only for workers' comp. I got **382 US firms** from four sources — NY WCB (74), CA DIR (63), the iapath IA directory (158, property/CAT), and your Dream 200 (125).

Two honest problems with that number:

- **120 of the 382 are workers'-comp TPAs.** Workers' comp is casualty, so they meet the letter of your definition, but a WC administrator is a different buyer from a property FNOL operation. Cozmo sells to the latter.
- **The CA roster includes self-administered self-insureds** — PG&E appears with 49 locations. Not a TPA. Needs filtering.

**Canada TPAs are effectively unbuilt** — 12 rows from research, every one flagged unverified. CIAA's member directory is search-only with no export.

Also: BCFSA, FSRA and AMF all publish provincial carrier lists, but behind JS/antibot interfaces curl can't reach. They need a browser session — probably another 50–100 small entities.

And none of these files have contact data. Company-level only; names, titles and emails are the next build.

The carrier side is done and I'd stand behind it. The TPA side needs either a browser-driven pass over state licensing portals and the CIAA directory, or a paid directory. Want me to run the browser pass?

### Alfred  
You caught a real flaw. New **P&L Model** tab is in the sheet (reopened in your browser), pushed as `f130dbf`.

## Answering your questions directly

**"Are the CEOs the same?"** At group level, yes — Liberty Mutual has one group CEO. **But that CEO is not who buys claims tech.** Underneath sit a Chief Claims Officer, VPs of Property / Auto / Commercial claims, and regional claims VPs. So:

**"Are the decision makers for that P&L the same?"** No. That's exactly where my 1,831 broke. The group count is right for **accounts** — who signs one contract — and wrong for **contacts**. I collapsed 69 entities to 1 org and implicitly to 1 buyer. Liberty Mutual is one account with roughly 30–45 budget owners in it.

**The unit isn't entities and it isn't groups. It's organisation size.** A 5-person Ontario farm mutual has 1–2 P&L owners. Liberty Mutual has dozens. Entity count tells you nothing about either.

## Your definition, applied

P&L owner = **controls their own budget line**. Budget authority, not seniority: CEO, MD, President, Owner, any Chief, VP at any level, GM, Treasurer. A GM who signs off on spend counts; an adjuster doesn't.

## The number

**7,076 – 11,968 unique P&L owners. Midpoint ~9,500**, across 2,402 organisations.

I didn't guess the multiplier — I measured it from our own harvest: 1,695 people across 113 companies, 1,279 of them P&L owners by that definition. Core P&C only, franchise networks excluded:

| Company headcount | Companies | Mean P&L owners |
|---|---|---|
| 10–50 | 16 | 2.5 |
| 50–200 | 18 | 5.3 |
| 200–1,000 | 17 | 11.2 |
| 1,000+ | 3 | 12.7 |

Two honest caveats. The harvest **capped near 125 people per company**, so large orgs are truncated and the real 1,000+ figure runs higher than 12.7. And only 3 companies sit in that top band, so it's the thinnest part of the curve.

One thing the data threw up that's worth keeping: I excluded franchise networks because SERVPRO showed 114 "P&L owners" — those aren't staff, they're **independent franchisees, each genuinely its own P&L.** Under your definition every one of them is a separate buyer. That's a real finding for the restoration campaign, not a data error.

## What it does to the funnel

9,522 contacts → 38,088 emails → **69 mailboxes** → ~190 replies → ~70 positive → **~32 meetings**.

Their existing 58 mailboxes nearly cover the 69 needed. At $100/meeting that's ~$3,200.

So the P&L view roughly doubles the contact count versus 5-per-org — but it lands in the same place on meetings, and it still doesn't reach 80–100. **Carriers and TPAs are a ~10K-contact universe, not a 34K one.** The volume you'd need for that promise is in restoration, where 60,000+ contractors each have an owner who is, by your definition, a P&L.

## What I'd missed

The NAIC PDF has a **Pools and Associations** section I never parsed: **500 entities** — 29 state FAIR plans, 10 coastal/beach & windstorm plans, 88 public entity pools, 81 state auto plans, 51 workers' comp plans. California FAIR Plan, Florida JUA, Texas Windstorm are serious property claim operations with real volume. They belong in the list and they weren't there. 141 are property-specific; the rest are auto/WC casualty.

## What I'm deliberately keeping out

**18,936 alien insurers.** That section is 916 pages, and it looks enormous until you see the domiciles: 9,677 Turks & Caicos, 1,722 Bermuda, 861 St Kitts, 746 Cayman. Offshore captives and reinsurance shells. They never touch a US property claim from a policyholder. Including them would inflate the universe roughly 7x with zero mailable buyers.

Also excluded: 1,529 US P&C entities in liquidation, rehab or conservatorship.

## The honest total

**2,902 companies built and named today. Realistic true universe 3,550–4,800** once the gaps close:

| Gap | Estimate |
|---|---|
| US TPAs / IA firms beyond the 382 found | 400–1,100 |
| MGAs / MGUs with delegated claims authority | 600–1,000 |
| Canada TPAs / adjusting firms | 100–200 |
| Canada provincial carriers (behind antibot) | 50–100 |

So your instinct was half right. The company count isn't small — I'd under-built it. But it also isn't 34,000. **Roughly 3,000 today, plausibly 4,000–4,800 fully built**, carrying 8,000–14,000 P&L owners. That's the real shape of the carrier + TPA market in the US and Canada.

The MGA gap is the one I'd chase next — MGAs with delegated claims authority are a genuine Cozmo buyer and there are more of them than TPAs.

## The filter I applied

Your test was "teams that get inbound calls." The measurable proxy is **direct property premium written to policyholders** — if a company writes property premium, someone answers the phone when a roof comes off. That drops reinsurers, offshore captives, and dormant shells without me guessing.

| Category | Orgs | How each was confirmed |
|---|---|---|
| US P&C carriers | **222** | Actual property premium in CA DOI + IL DOI market-share filings |
| US IA / CAT firms | 231 | Property/CAT adjusting directories |
| US residual-market pools | 134 | FAIR plans, windstorm, public entity pools |
| Canada P&C carriers | 124 | OSFI-authorized for the Property class |
| US TPAs (workers comp) | 116 | NY WCB + CA DIR registries |
| US TPAs (property claims) | 50 | NC DOI + Dream 200 |
| Canada mutuals | 42 | OMIA members |
| Canada TPAs / IA | 12 | Unverified — flagged in the row |

## What I found doing it

**California and Illinois both publish free market-share files with company names, NAIC codes and premium by line.** That's the unlock — 668 licensed entities confirmed writing property premium, rolling up to **222 real buying organisations**. State Farm General $3.7B, Farmers Exchange $1.4B, CSAA $1.06B, California Earthquake Authority $883M. Every one has a claims operation taking calls.

**NC's TPA directory was 512 firms and I kept 19.** It's their *life-and-health* licensing page — 280 were benefits administrators, pharmacy, dental. The 19 survivors are the right ones: AIG Claims, Broadspire, ESIS, Sedgwick, Glatfelter Claims Management, Avant Specialty Claims. This is the clearest evidence yet that state TPA registries mostly aren't P&C.

## Two things I want to be straight about

**222 carriers is a floor, not a ceiling.** It's confirmed from two states. A carrier writing only in Texas or Florida doesn't appear yet. Adding TX, FL and NY market-share files would likely push it to 400–600 — same method, just more downloads. Absence from this list isn't proof a company doesn't qualify.

**I could not get MGAs.** WSIA and TMPAA both put their member directories behind logins. I'm not going to invent names to fill that gap, so it's simply not in the file.

The 116 workers'-comp TPAs are tagged as such so you can exclude them in one filter click — casualty by the letter, but not your property FNOL buyer.

## What I added this round

**Texas** — TDI publishes per-line `.xls` files. Parsed 10 property lines: **478 companies**. State Farm Lloyds $4.35B, Allstate Vehicle & Property $2.67B, USAA $849M, Texas Windstorm Association $821M.

**Illinois** — 638 property writers, 634 matched.

**NAIC national market share report** (707pp, free) — covers all 58 jurisdictions, but it's Top 125 countrywide / Top 10 per state, so it names 185 groups rather than enumerating everything.

**US carriers confirmed: 222 → 269 organisations / 784 entities**, each row showing which states confirm it (263 IL-only, 201 TX+IL, 154 in all three).

## Two things I could not get, and won't fake

**Florida** — the file exists (OIR publishes company-level residential market share), but `floir.gov` refused the connection twice, once burning a 2-minute timeout. Retryable, not resolved.

**New York** — DFS does **not** publish company-level P&C premium. `data.ny.gov` has only statewide aggregate totals. There is no free NY equivalent of the CA/TX/IL files.

Also confirmed: **no single free national file lists every US P&C company with premium by state.** NAIC's is rankings; the complete data is behind paid iSite+/S&P. So "end to end complete" via free sources means union-of-states, and I have three of the four largest.

## On P&L holders — I did not multiply

You said don't estimate and don't use a multiplier, so I removed the multiplier entirely. The `PL OWNERS MEASURED` column now carries **only real counted numbers**: 57 organisations where we actually harvested and counted the people. The other 921 are **blank**, not modelled.

That is the honest state. A real per-company P&L count requires looking up each company — there's no way to derive it from premium or entity count without exactly the multiplier you rejected.

The tooling to close it is in place: Unipile with 7 connected LinkedIn accounts, plus an Apify token. Running it against 978 companies would give a genuine counted number per organisation. That's a background job, not a one-turn task.

Say the word and I'll start the enrichment pass, and retry Florida while it runs.
